extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato, classical education, and writers interested in philosophical principles of literary education
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and critique of Plato's educational theory and its implications for art, poetry, rhetoric, and lifelong self-education. Focuses on principles (simplicity, dialectic, abstraction), curriculum order, and moral effects of literature and drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as first principle of art and life
rubrics_metrics.description: The first principle which runs through all art and nature is simplicity; this also is to be the rule of human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity should be enforced across disciplines (music, gymnastic, law, medicine). Plato enforces simplicity in music and extends it to the training of the body; the legislator should restore law to simplicity and common sense. Implicitly, artistic production that is simple (clear, unadorned, proportioned) is preferable to excessive complication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit use of fiction in early education
rubrics_metrics.description: We should limit the use of fiction by the necessity of the case; a child must receive many lessons imperfectly understood and some in figure only, but fiction's use must be bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early instruction may use framed or figurative stories, but only insofar as necessary for the child's development. Dangerous examples (e.g., gods' lusts, treacheries, Homeric misbehaviour) should be banished or reformed so they do not serve as models for youth. The educator must weigh developmental appropriation against moral impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach simple moral and religious truths first
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Plato the aim of early education is not truth as a matter of fact, but truth as a matter of principle; the child is to be taught first simple religious truths, and then simple moral truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize foundational moral/religious principles that shape taste and manners before introducing complex factual or speculative material. This establishes a moral baseline for later literary/philosophical instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of drama's moral effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato is afraid of the influence of the drama, on the ground that it encourages false sentiment, and therefore he would not have his children taken to the theatre; he thinks that the effect on the spectators is bad, and on the actors still worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating dramatic writing or choosing dramatic influences for youth, consider whether works foster false sentiment or harmful imitation. Limit exposure of impressionable learners to theatre that may vitiate taste or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and separation of curriculum elements
rubrics_metrics.description: First stage: musical training (simplicity); second stage: gymnastic (muscular growth). The time of training is entirely separated from the time of literary education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato recommends distinct, orderly stages in education—musical (ethical/aesthetic formation) followed by physical training—avoiding simultaneous, conflicting trainings. While the text disagrees with strict separation, it presents curriculum sequencing as a deliberate pedagogical choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both music and physical training cultivate the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Music and gymnastic are not intended, the one for the cultivation of the mind and the other of the body, but they are both equally designed for the improvement of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design artistic and bodily practices to serve intellectual and moral ends; appreciate interdisciplinary effects (music, exercise contribute to mental formation and taste).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate abstraction through mathematical study
rubrics_metrics.description: The great aim of education is the cultivation of the habit of abstraction. This is to be acquired through the study of the mathematical sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To develop habits of abstraction—useful for high-level thought and for organizing ideas in rhetoric and literature—include mathematical or formal disciplines in advanced education. Mathematics trains relation-thinking and reduces the chaos of particulars to order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic as the highest method underpinning rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: The dialectician is as much above the mathematician as the mathematician is above the ordinary man. Dialectic ... divides a whole into the natural parts, and reunites the scattered parts into a natural or organized whole; which defines the abstract essences or universal ideas of all things, and connects them; which pierces the veil of hypotheses and reaches the final cause or first principle of all; which regards the sciences in relation to the idea of good. This ideal science is the highest process of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat dialectic (ordered questioning, analysis of essences, synthesis) as the methodological bedrock for persuasive speech and organized thought. For writers and rhetoricians, employ dialectical methods to classify, define, and connect concepts and to aim toward unifying ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop intellectual virtues: classification, proportion, unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The correlation of the sciences, the consciousness of the unity of nature, the idea of classification, the sense of proportion, the unwillingness to stop short of certainty or to confound probability with truth, are important principles of the higher education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train students to see connections across disciplines, to classify properly, to cultivate proportion and balance in judgment and composition, and to respect the difference between probability and truth—qualities that improve critical and creative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid doctrinaire one‑size‑fits‑all education
rubrics_metrics.description: He does not see that education is relative to the characters of individuals; he only desires to impress the same form of the state on the minds of all. After the Spartan fashion he would have his citizens cast in one mould; he does not seem to consider that some degree of freedom, 'a little wholesome neglect,' is necessary to strengthen and develope the character and to give play to the individual nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design educational and creative-training regimes that allow individual variation and freedom; resist uniform, doctrinaire models that suppress character and originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifelong self-education and choice of study
rubrics_metrics.description: The education of after life is necessarily the education which each one gives himself... That he shall choose the branch of knowledge to which his own mind most distinctly inclines, and in which he takes the greatest delight...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote continuous learning: encourage adults to pick subjects that align with their inclinations or contrast productively with daily work; self-directed study is central to mature intellectual and creative growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical self-education tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: He may study from the speculative side the profession or business in which he is practically engaged. He may make Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, Plato, Bacon the friends and companions of his life. He may find opportunities of hearing the living voice of a great teacher. He may select for enquiry some point of history or some unexplained phenomenon of nature. An hour a day passed in such scientific or literary pursuits will furnish as many facts as the memory can retain...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete recommendations for self-education: study your profession speculatively, read canonical masters, seek great teachers, pursue specific enquiries, and commit regular short periods (e.g., one hour/day) to sustained learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware vanity, crotchets, and overreaching schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Only let him beware of being the slave of crotchets, or of running after a Will o' the Wisp in his ignorance, or in his vanity of attributing to himself the gifts of a poet or assuming the air of a philosopher. He should know the limits of his own powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate self-knowledge and humility: avoid chasing fads, baseless enthusiasms, or pretending to skills one does not possess. Assess personal limits honestly when planning studies or creative projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build the mind by slow, steady additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Better to build up the mind by slow additions, to creep on quietly from one thing to another, to gain insensibly new powers and new interests in knowledge, than to form vast schemes which are never destined to be realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor incremental, sustained practice and modest goals over grandiose but unrealizable projects. Habitual, gradual accretion of knowledge and skill is the recommended strategy for lasting improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence and 'power of taking pains' as components of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius has been defined as 'the power of taking pains'; but hardly any one keeps up his interest in knowledge throughout a whole life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate creative promise not only by innate talent but by willingness to work, persist, and sacrifice. Encourage practices that maintain long-term intellectual curiosity and effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective censorship and moral responsibility of poets
rubrics_metrics.description: The old enmity to the poets... [they] are peremptorily ordered out of the city, if they are not willing to submit their poems to the censorship of the magistrates (Rep.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's view: literary works should be subject to moral scrutiny and, if necessary, excluded when they undermine civic virtue. When considering the role of poets, weigh moral influence and the possibility of regulating harmful content.
